summary.text: Define suffix-mass deficits from the all-ones target; they evolve by taking the floor of the average of neighboring deficits, and stabilization occurs exactly when the last relevant deficit vanishes because zeros propagate leftward. A coupling showing that the deficits for masses \(n\) and \(n+1\) differ by at most one, together with a shifted zero-propagation invariant, proves that the latter cannot stabilize by time \(a(n)\) but must stabilize by time \(a(n)+2\), giving the two possible increments.

full_proof.text:
Let all cell positions be indexed by the nonnegative integers, beginning with position 0. For a finite configuration \(c=(c_0,c_1,\dots)\), missing entries are understood to be zero. One update replaces it by the configuration whose mass at position \(i\) is
\[
 c_i'=\left\lceil\frac{c_i}{2}\right\rceil+
 \begin{cases}
 0,&i=0,\\[2mm]
 \left\lfloor\frac{c_{i-1}}2\right\rfloor,&i>0.
 \end{cases}
\]
Trailing zero entries are then deleted. Starting from the one-cell configuration \((n)\), let \(S_{n,t}\) be the configuration after \(t\) updates. Thus \(a(n)\) is the least \(t\) for which \(S_{n,t}\) is the configuration consisting of \(n\) ones.

We prove that, for every \(n\geq 1\),
\[
 a(n)+1\leq a(n+1)\leq a(n)+2.
\]
Since all these quantities are integers, this is precisely the assertion that
\[
 a(n+1)=a(n)+1\quad\hbox{or}\quad a(n+1)=a(n)+2.
\]

## 1. Suffix sums

For a finite configuration \(c\), define its suffix sum at position \(j\) by
\[
 T(c,j)=\sum_{i\geq j}c_i.
\]
Deleting trailing zeros does not change any suffix sum. The crucial observation is the following update formula:
\[
 T(c',j)=\left\lfloor\frac{T(c,j-1)+T(c,j)}2\right\rfloor,                 \tag{1}
\]
where at \(j=0\) we interpret \(j-1\) as 0.

To see this, first suppose \(j>0\). In the new suffix beginning at \(j\), the cells originally at positions \(i\geq j\) contribute their retained masses \(\lceil c_i/2\rceil\), while the cells originally at positions \(i\geq j-1\) contribute the masses \(\lfloor c_i/2\rfloor\) sent to the right. Hence
\[
 T(c',j)=\sum_{i\geq j}\left\lceil\frac{c_i}{2}\right\rceil
       +\sum_{i\geq j-1}\left\lfloor\frac{c_i}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
For every \(x\),
\[
 \left\lceil\frac x2\right\rceil+\left\lfloor\frac x2\right\rfloor=x.
\]
Thus all terms from positions \(i\geq j\) combine to \(T(c,j)\), leaving an additional \(\lfloor c_{j-1}/2\rfloor\). Since
\(c_{j-1}=T(c,j-1)-T(c,j)\), this is equal to
\[
 T(c,j)+\left\lfloor\frac{T(c,j-1)-T(c,j)}2\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{T(c,j-1)+T(c,j)}2\right\rfloor.
\]
For \(j=0\), formula (1) says that the total mass after an update is the total mass before the update, which follows from the same identity between floor and ceiling. This proves (1).

Write
\[
 C(n,t,j)=T(S_{n,t},j).
\]
Initially there is mass \(n\) only at position 0, so
\[
 C(n,0,j)=
 \begin{cases}
 n,&j=0,\\
 0,&j>0.
 \end{cases}                                                     \tag{2}
\]
By (1),
\[
 C(n,t+1,j)=\left\lfloor
 \frac{C(n,t,j-1)+C(n,t,j)}2
 \right\rfloor.                                                  \tag{3}
\]

The stable configuration \((1,\dots,1)\) of length \(n\) has suffix sums
\[
 n-j:=\max(n-j,0).
\]
Conversely, among finite configurations with no trailing zero, these suffix sums characterize that configuration. Indeed, if all suffix sums equal \(n-j\), the total sum is \(n\), the sum after deleting the first entry is \(n-1\), and hence the first entry is 1. Applying the same argument successively to the remaining suffix gives one 1 at each of positions \(0,\dots,n-1\), and zero suffix sum thereafter. The absence of a trailing zero rules out any extra listed cells. Every state \(S_{n,t}\), for \(n>0\), has no trailing zero because trailing zeros are deleted after each update (and the initial one-cell state is nonzero). Therefore
\[
 S_{n,t}=(\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{n\text{ times}})
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 C(n,t,j)=n-j\text{ for every }j.                                 \tag{4}
\]

## 2. Deficits

We first note that
\[
 C(n,t,j)\leq n-j                                                    \tag{5}
\]
for every \(n,t,j\). This follows by induction on \(t\). It is immediate from (2). For the induction step, use (3). At \(j=0\), total mass is conserved, so the bound is \(C(n,t+1,0)\leq n\). If \(j>0\), the two induction bounds are \(n-(j-1)\) and \(n-j\). When \(j\leq n\), these are respectively \((n-j)+1\) and \(n-j\), whose average has floor \(n-j\). When \(j>n\), the relevant bounds are zero, so the conclusion again follows.

Define the nonnegative deficit
\[
 D(n,t,j)=(n-j)-C(n,t,j).                                         \tag{6}
\]
By (2), its initial values are
\[
 D(n,0,j)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&j=0,\\
 n-j,&j>0.
 \end{cases}                                                     \tag{7}
\]
A direct substitution of (3) into (6), using (5) to justify the ordinary nonnegative differences, gives the same averaging recurrence:
\[
 D(n,t+1,j)=\left\lfloor
 \frac{D(n,t,j-1)+D(n,t,j)}2
 \right\rfloor.                                                  \tag{8}
\]
At \(j=0\), both occurrences of \(j-1\) mean 0, so this says simply that the boundary deficit remains unchanged. In particular,
\[
 D(n,t,0)=0                                                       \tag{9}
\]
for all \(t\). Also, directly from (6),
\[
 0\leq D(n,t,j)\leq n-j,                                        \tag{10}
\]
and consequently
\[
 D(n,t,j)=0\qquad(j\geq n).                                     \tag{11}
\]
By (4) and (6), stabilization is equivalent to all deficits being zero:
\[
 S_{n,t}=(1,\dots,1)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 D(n,t,j)=0\text{ for every }j.                                  \tag{12}
\]

We now establish three structural properties of these deficits.

### Lemma 1: coupling consecutive masses

For all \(n,t,j\),
\[
 D(n,t,j)\leq D(n+1,t,j)\leq D(n,t,j)+1.                         \tag{13}
\]

At time zero this follows immediately from (7): increasing \(n\) to \(n+1\) changes each initial deficit by either 0 or 1. Suppose (13) holds at time \(t\), at both positions \(j-1\) and \(j\). Thus each of the two inputs for the \((n+1)\)-system lies between the corresponding input for the \(n\)-system and that input plus 1. Adding the two inequalities and dividing by 2 shows that the floors of the two averages differ by either 0 or 1. Recurrence (8) therefore gives (13) at time \(t+1\). This proves the coupling by induction.

### Lemma 2: a zero propagates to the left

If
\[
 1\leq j\leq n-1\quad\text{and}\quad D(n,t,j)=0,
\]
then
\[
 D(n,t,j-1)=0.                                                    \tag{14}
\]

We prove this by induction on \(t\). At time zero, (7) says that for \(1\leq j\leq n-1\), the deficit is \(n-j>0\), so the hypothesis cannot occur.

For the induction step, suppose \(D(n,t+1,j)=0\). By (8),
\[
 D(n,t,j-1)+D(n,t,j)\leq 1.                                     \tag{15}
\]
If \(j=1\), the desired conclusion is simply (9). Assume \(j\geq2\). We claim first that \(D(n,t,j-1)=0\). Otherwise it is at least 1, so (15) forces \(D(n,t,j)=0\). Applying the induction hypothesis at position \(j\) would then give \(D(n,t,j-1)=0\), a contradiction. Thus \(D(n,t,j-1)=0\). Applying the induction hypothesis once more, now at position \(j-1\), yields \(D(n,t,j-2)=0\). Recurrence (8) at position \(j-1\) now gives
\[
 D(n,t+1,j-1)=\left\lfloor\frac{0+0}{2}\right\rfloor=0.
\]
This proves (14).

It follows by repeated application that if the last relevant deficit vanishes, then all deficits vanish:
\[
 D(n,t,n-1)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D(n,t,j)=0\text{ for every }j. \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, Lemma 2 moves the zero successively left from \(n-1\) to 0, while (11) handles every \(j\geq n\).

### Lemma 3: shifted draining between consecutive systems

If
\[
 j+1\leq n-1\quad\text{and}\quad D(n,t,j+1)=0,

afterward
\[
 D(n+1,t,j)=0.                                                    \tag{17}
\]

Again use induction on \(t\). At time zero the hypothesis, by (7), forces \(n-(j+1)=0\), contrary to \(j+1\leq n-1\); hence the assertion is vacuous.

Suppose now that \(D(n,t+1,j+1)=0\). By (8),
\[
 D(n,t,j)+D(n,t,j+1)\leq1.                                      \tag{18}
\]
We first show \(D(n,t,j)=0\). If \(D(n,t,j+1)>0\), this follows immediately from (18). If \(D(n,t,j+1)=0\), it follows from Lemma 2. If \(j=0\), conclusion (17) is just the boundary identity (9) for the \((n+1)\)-system. If \(j>0\), apply the induction hypothesis, with \(j-1\) in place of \(j\), to the equality \(D(n,t,j)=0\). This gives
\[
 D(n+1,t,j-1)=0.                                                 \tag{19}
\]
On the other hand, the coupling (13) and \(D(n,t,j)=0\) give
\[
 D(n+1,t,j)\leq1.                                                \tag{20}
\]
Using (19), (20), and recurrence (8),
\[
 D(n+1,t+1,j)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{D(n+1,t,j-1)+D(n+1,t,j)}2\right\rfloor
 =0.
\]
This completes the proof of Lemma 3.

## 3. Draining the \((n+1)\)-system within two further steps

Suppose \(n\geq1\), and at some time \(A\) the entire \(n\)-system is drained:
\[
 D(n,A,j)=0\quad\text{for every }j.                              \tag{21}
\]
We claim that
\[
 D(n+1,A+2,n)=0.                                                  \tag{22}
\]

First consider position \(n-1\) in the \((n+1)\)-system at time \(A+1\). We need its two inputs at time \(A\). The left input is position \(n-2\). If \(n=1\), this is interpreted as boundary position 0 and has deficit zero by (9). If \(n\geq2\), Lemma 3, applied to the zero \(D(n,A,n-1)=0\) from (21), gives
\[
 D(n+1,A,n-2)=0.                                                 \tag{23}
\]
The other input obeys, by coupling and (21),
\[
 D(n+1,A,n-1)\leq D(n,A,n-1)+1=1.                               \tag{24}
\]
Therefore (8), (23), and (24) imply
\[
 D(n+1,A+1,n-1)=0.                                               \tag{25}
\]

At position \(n\), coupling and (11) give
\[
 D(n+1,A+1,n)\leq D(n,A+1,n)+1=1.                               \tag{26}
\]
A final use of (8), with (25) and (26), yields
\[
 D(n+1,A+2,n)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{D(n+1,A+1,n-1)+D(n+1,A+1,n)}2\right\rfloor
 =0,
\]
which is (22).

This also proves that every positive-mass system eventually stabilizes. Indeed, use induction on \(n\). For \(n=1\), the initial configuration is already stable, and all deficits are zero at time 0. If the \(n\)-system is fully drained at some time \(A\), (22) says that the last relevant deficit of the \((n+1)\)-system vanishes at time \(A+2\). By (16), all its deficits then vanish. Thus the set of stabilization times is nonempty for every \(n\geq1\).

By (12) and (16), we may consequently characterize the stopping time solely through the last relevant deficit:
\[
 a(n)=\min\{t:D(n,t,n-1)=0\}.                                   \tag{27}
\]
In particular,
\[
 D(n,a(n),n-1)=0,                                                \tag{28}
\]
and this deficit is nonzero at every earlier time:
\[
 t<a(n)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D(n,t,n-1)\geq1.               \tag{29}
\]
Moreover, (16) and (28) show that at time \(a(n)\),
\[
 D(n,a(n),j)=0\quad\text{for every }j.                           \tag{30}
\]

## 4. Comparison of the two stopping times

Fix \(n\geq1\), and put \(A=a(n)\).

First we prove that the \((n+1)\)-system cannot stabilize by time \(A\). More precisely,
\[
 D(n+1,t,n)\geq1\qquad(0\leq t\leq A).                           \tag{31}
\]
We prove this by induction on \(t\). At time 0, formula (7) gives
\[
 D(n+1,0,n)=(n+1)-n=1.
\]
Now suppose \(t+1\leq A\) and \(D(n+1,t,n)\geq1\). Then \(t<A\), so (29) gives
\[
 D(n,t,n-1)\geq1.
\]
By the lower half of the coupling inequality (13),
\[
 D(n+1,t,n-1)\geq D(n,t,n-1)\geq1.
\]
Both inputs in recurrence (8) for \(D(n+1,t+1,n)\) are therefore at least 1. Hence
\[
 D(n+1,t+1,n)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{D(n+1,t,n-1)+D(n+1,t,n)}2\right\rfloor
 \geq1.
\]
This proves (31). Since stabilization of the \((n+1)\)-system requires its last relevant deficit \(D(n+1,t,n)\) to vanish, (31) implies
\[
 a(n+1)\geq A+1=a(n)+1.                                         \tag{32}
\]

For the upper bound, (30) says that the \(n\)-system is fully drained at time \(A\). Applying the two-step draining result (22) gives
\[
 D(n+1,A+2,n)=0.
\]
By (16), the whole \((n+1)\)-system is then drained, and hence stable. Therefore
\[
 a(n+1)\leq A+2=a(n)+2.                                         \tag{33}
\]

Combining (32) and (33),
\[
 a(n)+1\leq a(n+1)\leq a(n)+2.
\]
The quantities are integers, so exactly one of the two possibilities holds:
\[
 \boxed{a(n+1)=a(n)+1\quad\text{or}\quad a(n+1)=a(n)+2.}
\]
This is valid for every integer \(n\geq1\), as required.
